description: Somos ingenieros de sistemas participando en el reto Be An Earth System Trend Detective del NASA Space Apps Challenge. Nuestro objetivo es crear una herramienta que procese y visualice datos científicos de la Tierra para detectar tendencias ambientales globales. Tenemos conocimientos en desarrollo de software, arquitectura e ingeniería de datos. Buscamos miembros interesados en ciencia de datos, mapeo SIG, diseño UI UX o redacción para complementar el equipo y construir una soluciones de impacto
summary: Peru Trend Detective (Detective del Perú) is a map that shows what is changing in each region of Peru. Pick rainfall, temperature or vegetation (NDVI), tap one of the 25 departments, and see how it changed from 2001 to 2024: how much it changed per decade, whether the trend is statistically significant, and a plain-language verdict: "real change", "possibly chance" or "not enough data". The same variable can rise in one region and fall in another, so the map shows both at once. The data comes from NASA POWER, GPM IMERG and MODIS, analyzed with the Mann-Kendall test, Sen's slope and the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple tests. Rainfall trends can also be checked without El Niño years, which can create or hide a trend on the coast. For irrigated valleys like Chavimochic and Ica, a before-and-after NDVI slider shows how the green area grew. It is built for farmers and students: each one sees the same data, explained in their own way. It does not forecast or recommend actions, and every number is precalculated from NASA data.
details:
Peru Trend Detective

See what has really changed in your part of Peru, using NASA data from 2001 to 2024.

What it does

Peru Trend Detective is a map of Peru's 25 departments (the country's main regions). You pick rainfall, temperature or vegetation, tap a department, and the app tells you three things: how much it changed between 2001 and 2024, how sure we can be about it, and what that means in everyday words.

We built it because in Peru the same variable can go up in one region and down in another. One national number hides that. On our map you see both at once, and every department gets an honest answer: real change, possibly chance or not enough data.

The home page starts with a simple question: who are you? A farmer and a student need the same facts, told in different ways. You choose how you want them explained, and the numbers stay the same for everyone.

Using it as a farmer

Tap Puno and the answer comes first, in plain words: it rains more than in 2001, and "this is already happening", not just one lucky year. A needle shows whether there is less rain, the same or more, and how far it could go.

Below that come the questions people in the field actually ask. Are dry years coming more often? What does El Niño, the warming of the Pacific Ocean that hits Peru every few years, usually bring here? What does a normal year look like, in millimeters and in cubic meters of water per hectare? We also point to SENAMHI, Peru's national weather service, and ENFEN, the national committee that issues the official El Niño alerts.

For heat we don't talk about degrees per decade. We use a comparison anyone in the Andes understands. Apurímac is about 1.1 °C warmer than in 2001, which is like having your field about 180 meters lower down the mountain. Very hot years went from 3 out of 12 to 10 out of 12.

Vegetation comes from MODIS satellite images. In the Chavimochic valley, green fields grew from about 18,900 to 35,600 hectares between 2001 and 2024. You can drag a slider to compare both years. The app also says why: it is mostly new irrigation, not more rain.

Using it as a student

The same tap on Puno now shows the numbers behind the answer: +141 mm per decade, a likely range of +42 to +251 mm, the p and q values, and a chart with every year, the trend line and the El Niño years marked.

We also show when the data does not agree. NASA POWER says Puno is getting wetter, while the GPM IMERG satellite record says it is getting drier. We don't hide that. Both appear side by side, with the reason: the satellites changed in 2014, so we use IMERG to compare, never to call a change real.

"Does the result hold?" checks the same trend without El Niño years and over a longer period that starts in 1981. In Puno the change is still real without El Niño, but over the longer period it no longer passes, so the app says "use with care". A ranking places each department next to all the others.

Students can take everything with them: a CSV table with the source written at the top, the chart as an image, a full PDF report, a ready citation in APA or BibTeX, and a link that opens exactly the same view.

Traveling through the years

"By year" shows a single year instead of the trend. In 2017, when a strong El Niño hit the north coast, Piura got 167% more rain than usual. Press play and the years go by on the map.

How it works

A Python pipeline downloads the NASA data, averages it for each department and calculates the trends once. The results are saved as files, and a small API written in Rust only serves them. Nothing is calculated live, so every number can be checked and repeated.

For each department we use the yearly averages and run a Mann-Kendall test (with pre-whitening, a fix for the fact that one year often looks like the next), Sen's slope per decade and a 95% confidence range. Since we test 25 departments at the same time, we correct the results with the Benjamini-Hochberg method, so a few lucky results don't look like real changes. We only say real change when three things are true: q is below 0.05, the confidence range does not cross zero, and each year is not too similar to the one before. Everything else is possibly chance. With fewer than 20 years or fewer than 4 grid cells, it is not enough data.

The methodology page explains all of this in simple language, with the sources, a glossary, the limits and the scientific references.

What we found

  • 11 departments got warmer with a real change, between about 0.26 and 0.77 °C per decade. None got cooler.
  • Rainfall changed for real in 5 departments. It went up in Ica, La Libertad and Puno, and down in Loreto and Ucayali. Up in one place, down in another.
  • 14 departments got greener with a real change. None got less green.
  • For many departments the honest answer is "we can't tell yet", and the app says exactly that.

Who it is for, and why it matters

We made it for two groups: farmers who want to know if what they feel in the field shows up in the data, and students, especially in environmental engineering, who need clean, citable numbers for their work. Neither group should need a statistics course to read NASA data.

It works on a phone, in Spanish and English, and it can be used with a keyboard or a screen reader. If the free server is asleep, the app uses a local copy of the same data so nobody is left waiting.

What makes it different

  • The map itself tells the story. In 3D, each department rises where it rains more and sinks where it rains less.
  • Same data, two voices. The farmer and the student see the same numbers, explained in their own language.
  • It is honest about doubt. It shows when a change could be chance and when two NASA sources disagree, instead of picking the most dramatic number.
  • It shows the past, not the future. It does not forecast or tell anyone what to do. Every figure goes back to a NASA source.

Things we kept in mind

  • A department is a big area, so we remind people that their own field may be different.
  • El Niño can create or hide a trend on the coast, so you can always remove those years and compare.
  • Some places need extra care. Olmos mixes new farmland with dry forest, and in the rainforest NDVI is already close to its maximum, so small changes are hard to see. Those places carry a clear warning.
  • Large buttons for touch screens, good contrast, and less movement for people who turn animations off.

Tools we used

Python (xarray, SciPy, pymannkendall, earthaccess) for the data, Rust with Axum for the API, React 19 with TypeScript and Vite for the website, three.js for the 3D map, Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui for the design, Recharts for the charts, and Vitest and Playwright for testing, all checked on every change with GitHub Actions. The site runs on Vercel and the API on Render. No special hardware, just our laptops.



Source code

Both repositories are public, so anyone can check the code and repeat every number.

  • Website (frontend): github.com/unac-team-challenges/nasa-challenge-frontend
  • Data pipeline and API (backend): github.com/unac-team-challenges/nasa-challenge-backend
